newsitem.title: USA: TWA crash investigators to scrape ocean floor.
newsitem.headline: TWA crash investigators to scrape ocean floor.

text.p: After more than three months searching for clues to the TWA Flight 800 crash, investigators said on Monday they will scrape up the underwater crash site in hopes of finding the key to the disaster.

The decision to trawl the ocean bottom, using rakes to dig up six to 12 inches (15-30 cm) of the sea floor, marks a turning point in the investigation because the process will irretrievably damage the crash site, said Robert Francis, vice chairman of the National Transportation Safety Board.
With trawling, he told a media briefing, "you have so disturbed the environment that the chances of finding anything after that are fairly minimal."

Investigators also have decided to return all of the victims' possessions to their families, said James Kallstrom, chief FBI investigator, at the same briefing. Forensic testing on their personal effects has been completed, he said.
"There's no reason from the standpoint of the investigation" not to return them, Kallstrom said.
Investigators too have decided to build a larger and more comprehensive mockup of the area around the Boeing 747's centre fuel tank, which is known to have exploded.

As with the other developments, the mockup marks a point of no return because it will use pieces of the plane's debris in such a way that they will no longer be available for more minute, individual study, investigators said.

As investigators head into the latest stages of the probe, they say they still do not know why the Paris-bound jet exploded and crashed into the Atlantic Ocean off the coast of Long Island, New York, just minutes after taking off on July 17 from Kennedy International Airport.
All 230 people on board died in the disaster, which investigators believe was caused either by a bomb, a missile or mechanical failure.
Looking weary, Francis, who noted that the day's media briefing was the 86th news conference the NTSB has held since the crash, said trawling could begin by the end of the week.

The trawling, which would cover a one-third by one-half mile (0.4 by 0.8 km) site, is intended to find the plane's last bits of wreckage, he said. More than 95 percent of the downed plane has been recovered.
In particular, investigators say they would like to find the scavenge pump, designed to pull the dregs from the centre tank, and several pieces of the plane's centre fuel tank.

Investigators also will decide whether to blow up a similar fuel tank or another Boeing 747 after experiments on jet fuel volatitily are completed at California Institute of Technology in Pasadena, California.

Investigators say there were 50 to 100 gallons (190-380 litres) of jet fuel in the centre tank, and normally the electrical current in any of the nearby equipment would not be strong enough to spark such a devastating explosion.

Kallstrom minimised the significance of an unidentified duffel bag that showed unusual rips and tears and which investigators had been questioning victims' families about. He said the bag was not connected to any type of high explosive device but investigators wanted to know where it had been located on the plane.
"It's not an item of great importance," he said.
Investigators also questioned victims' families about the identitiy of a person whose name had seemingly appeared among the debris but was not on the passenger manifest, he said.
That person has proven to be unconnected to the flight, he said. The name was retrieved in material that was floating and recovered along the shore of New Jersey, he said.
